title: AI Agent Permission and Tool-Use Security Review
summary: Find out what your AI agents can actually do: which tools, credentials and money-moving actions they reach, where approvals sit, and whether injected text can make them misuse tools.

seo.title: AI Agent Permission and Tool-Use Review | VipraTech
seo.description: Security review of AI agents and MCP tools in payments: permission mapping, approval gates on refunds and payouts, and tool-misuse testing in staging.

problem.intro: Payment companies are giving agents real permissions: issuing refunds under a limit, updating merchant records, querying ledgers, triaging disputes, or acting through MCP servers wired to internal systems. The risk moves from what the model says to what it does. One over-scoped service account or missing approval step can turn a prompt injection into a payout.

pain_points.title: Over-scoped credentials
pain_points.detail: Agents often run on a shared service account with far more access than any single task needs.

pain_points.title: Missing approval gates
pain_points.detail: Irreversible actions such as refunds, payout releases or changes to a merchant's settlement account run without a human or second check.

pain_points.title: Injection reaching tools
pain_points.detail: Text in tickets, emails or merchant notes can steer an agent into calling tools in ways nobody intended.

pain_points.title: Weak audit trail
pain_points.detail: Logs show that an API was called, but not which agent called it, on whose behalf, or why.

solution.overview: We review your agents the way an attacker and an auditor would. First we build an inventory: every agent, every tool and MCP server it can call, the credentials behind each tool and the actions those credentials allow, including any that move money or change payout details. We compare this with what each agent actually needs and mark the excess. Then we test in staging: planting instructions in tickets, emails and data fields, attempting cross-merchant actions, chaining tools and pushing past limits. You get a permission matrix, validated findings with tool-call traces, and concrete controls such as scoped tokens, transaction limits enforced outside the model, allowlists and human approval on high-impact actions.
capabilities: Inventory of agents, tools, MCP servers, credentials and reachable actions
Least-privilege gap analysis per agent and per tool
Review of approval gates, limits and kill switches on money-moving and account-changing actions
Adversarial testing for goal hijack, tool misuse and indirect prompt injection in staging
Audit log review covering agent identity, on-behalf-of user, inputs and tool calls
Control recommendations with example policies and code-level fixes

workflow.title: Inventory
workflow.detail: We document each agent, its tools and MCP servers, the credentials used and the actions each credential allows.

workflow.title: Mark high-impact actions
workflow.detail: Refunds, payouts, settlement account changes, KYC status changes and bulk data exports are tagged as high-impact.

workflow.title: Gap analysis
workflow.detail: Granted permissions are compared with what each task needs, and missing approvals or limits are recorded.

workflow.title: Adversarial testing
workflow.detail: In staging, we attempt goal hijack, cross-merchant actions and injected instructions through realistic data channels.

workflow.title: Validate findings
workflow.detail: Each issue is reproduced and rated by impact, with the tool-call trace as evidence.

workflow.title: Controls and retest
workflow.detail: We recommend specific controls, review your fixes and retest the high-impact paths.

inputs: List of agents and their intended tasks
Tool definitions, MCP server configurations and API specifications
IAM roles, service accounts and token scopes
Staging environment with test merchants and customers
outputs: Permission matrix per agent, tool and credential
List of high-impact actions with their current controls
human_in_the_loop: Our testers validate every finding before it is reported. Your security, engineering and payment operations leads decide which controls to apply, and we recommend human approval on any action that moves money or changes payout details.
integrations: Agent frameworks such as LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK or custom orchestrators
MCP servers and internal tool APIs
Cloud IAM and secrets managers on AWS, Azure, GCP or Vault
Logging and SIEM such as Splunk, Elastic or Datadog
Jira for findings and remediation tracking
guardrails: Testing only in staging with test merchants and synthetic balances
No real refunds, payouts or account changes triggered at any point
Read-only access to IAM and configuration during discovery
Written stop conditions for any unexpected effect outside staging
Evidence encrypted and deleted at the end of the retention period
compliance_notes: Supports the accountability and human oversight practices recommended in RBI's FREE-AI framework.
Findings map to excessive agency and related risks in the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications.

pilot.scope: One agent with real tool access, such as a refund or dispute triage agent, reviewed end to end with one retest.

what_we_measure.how: Granted actions not needed by the agent's defined tasks, counted per tool.
Money-moving or account-changing actions that run without a human or second check.
Validated paths from untrusted input to a high-impact tool call.
Findings confirmed fixed versus still open after remediation.

faqs.q: We use a vendor's agent platform. Can you still review it?
faqs.a: Yes, as far as its configuration and permissions are visible to you. We review the tools, credentials and approval settings you control and test behaviour in your staging tenant.
Yes. MCP servers are tools with their own permissions and inputs, so we include them in the inventory and test whether an agent can be steered into misusing them.
No. All testing runs in staging with test merchants and synthetic balances, under written rules of engagement.

faqs.q: What baseline controls do you recommend?
faqs.a: Scoped, per-task credentials, hard transaction limits enforced outside the model, and human approval for refunds above a limit, payouts and payout-detail changes. The model should never be the only thing between an instruction and a money movement.
